title: Indian Students Going Abroad for Higher Education Drop 31% in Two Years
excerpt: Government data presented in Parliament shows the number of Indians pursuing studies overseas fell from 908,000 in 2023 to 626,000 in 2025, reversing a post-pandemic surge as visa rules tighten and costs rise across major destinations.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Indian students abroad dropped from 908,000 in 2023 to 626,000 in 2025, a 31% decline.
  • Visa restrictions and rising costs in Canada, UK, and Australia are major factors for the downturn.
  • The Indian government promotes domestic education reforms as alternatives to studying abroad.
  • Western universities may face revenue challenges due to decreased Indian student enrollment.

A Sharp Reversal in Outbound Mobility

The number of Indian students travelling overseas for higher education has fallen for the third consecutive year, according to new government data presented in India's upper house of Parliament, the Rajya Sabha.

Minister of State for Education Sukanta Majumdar told lawmakers that 626,000 Indian students went abroad for studies in 2025, down from 770,000 in 2024 and 908,000 in 2023. The data, sourced from the Union Home Ministry's Bureau of Immigration, tracks Indian nationals who listed study or education as their purpose of travel.

The overall decline of approximately 282,000 students over two years amounts to a 31% drop from the 2023 peak — a sharp reversal of the post-pandemic surge that had made India one of the largest source countries for international students worldwide.

Visa Walls Going Up Across the West

While the parliamentary reply did not cite specific reasons for the downturn, the decline tracks closely with a wave of immigration policy changes across India's top study destinations.

Canada, which saw the steepest fall, recorded a 41% drop in Indian student arrivals between 2023 and 2024 alone. Ottawa has capped international student permits, raised financial proof requirements, and tightened post-graduation work permit eligibility. The UK saw a 27% decline over the same period, with 76% of British universities reporting reduced Indian enrollment in the January 2026 intake, according to a survey by the British Universities International Liaison Association.

In the United States, the F-1 visa rejection rate for Indian applicants hit 41% in 2025, the highest in a decade. SEVIS data shows Indian student numbers in the US fell 6.9% to 352,644 by February 2026 — the largest single-year drop since the COVID-19 disruption. Australia has similarly raised financial eligibility thresholds and tightened compliance requirements.

"Families aren't quitting. They're calculating."

— Vijay Kumar Chaudhary, Education Consultant

Rising Costs, Falling Returns

Beyond visa barriers, the financial calculus has shifted. Tuition fees at universities in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia have continued to climb, while the Indian rupee's depreciation against major currencies has amplified costs further. A course priced at $50,000 becomes roughly ₹50,000 more expensive with every one-rupee decline against the dollar.

An HSBC survey found that Indian families are placing greater emphasis on return on investment, weighing whether a foreign degree will translate into stable employment. With post-study work pathways becoming less predictable across multiple countries, the risk-reward ratio has tilted against studying abroad for many middle-class families.

Education experts note that students are increasingly deferring admissions, switching destination countries, or withdrawing applications altogether when costs rise unexpectedly or visa rules shift before departure.

India Bets on Domestic Alternatives

The government has framed the decline partly as a consequence of improving domestic options. Majumdar told Parliament that the administration has taken steps under the National Education Policy 2020 to strengthen higher education within India, including upgrading infrastructure, reforming accreditation, promoting research and innovation, and expanding digital education.

A notable policy shift allows foreign universities to establish campuses in India. So far, 14 foreign institutions have received approval, while five overseas universities have been cleared to operate in GIFT City, Gujarat. Institutions including Deakin University, the University of Wollongong, the University of Southampton, and the Illinois Institute of Technology have announced or begun offering courses in India.

In the latest QS World University Rankings for 2027, 12 Indian universities featured in the global top 500, the country's best-ever performance, lending credibility to the domestic alternative narrative.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, the trend carries mixed signals. Families with children in the pipeline for overseas education face a landscape of higher costs, stricter visa regimes, and less certain post-study employment. The traditional pathway — study abroad, secure a work visa, settle — is no longer as straightforward as it was even three years ago.

At the same time, the growth of foreign university campuses in India and improving domestic institutions may offer a middle path: global-standard credentials without the financial and immigration risks of relocating.

Majumdar characterized overseas education as a matter of "individual will and choice," shaped by affordability, access to education loans, exposure to foreign societies, and suitability for particular disciplines. He added that the government views its globally placed workforce and diaspora as national assets — a framing that suggests New Delhi sees value in outbound mobility even as the numbers decline.

What's Next

With Western universities increasingly dependent on Indian enrollment revenue and India simultaneously tightening its own international education strategy, the next academic cycle will be closely watched. If the decline stabilizes, it may reflect a new equilibrium. If it accelerates, universities from London to Toronto to Sydney will face serious revenue shortfalls — and India's bet on domestic education will face its biggest test yet.
